source_note: Original operating summaries inspired by common public mental-model lists and decision-making literature.

models.title: Second-Order Thinking
models.summary: Evaluate the consequences of the consequences before choosing an action.
models.use_when: A decision has delayed effects, incentives, dependencies, or social consequences.
questions: What happens immediately if this works?
What happens six weeks later?
Who changes behavior because of this decision?
What new problem does the solution create?
models.action: Write first-order, second-order, and third-order effects before committing.
models.failure: Stopping at the obvious benefit and missing the downstream cost.

models.title: Inversion
models.summary: Solve backwards by asking what would guarantee failure, then avoid it.
models.use_when: The desired outcome is vague but the failure modes are easier to identify.
questions: What would make this fail predictably?
What am I assuming must go right?
Which mistake is irreversible?
What should I stop doing first?
models.action: List the top failure paths and convert each into a prevention rule.
models.failure: Using inversion as pessimism instead of operational risk control.

models.title: Regret Minimization
models.summary: Choose by asking which option your future self is least likely to regret.
models.use_when: A decision has emotional weight, uncertainty, or a long time horizon.
questions: At age 80, what would I wish I had tried?
Which regret is recoverable?
Which regret compounds if ignored?
Am I avoiding discomfort or avoiding real risk?
models.action: Write the reversible and irreversible regrets, then pick the option with the better long-term regret profile.
models.failure: Romanticizing bold action when the real issue is unpriced downside.

models.title: 10-10-10 Rule
models.summary: View a choice through three time windows: 10 minutes, 10 months, and 10 years.
models.use_when: Emotion is dominating a decision or a short-term discomfort hides long-term value.
questions: How will this feel in 10 minutes?
What will matter in 10 months?
What will still matter in 10 years?
Which time window deserves priority here?
models.action: Score each option across the three windows and explain the tradeoff explicitly.
models.failure: Pretending every decision deserves a 10-year lens.

models.title: Goodharts Law
models.summary: When a measure becomes the target, it stops being a reliable measure.
models.use_when: You are optimizing a metric, KPI, habit score, leaderboard, or proxy signal.
questions: What is the real goal behind this metric?
How could someone game it?
What behavior does this metric reward?
What qualitative signal should stay visible?
models.action: Pair every target metric with a counter-metric and a human review rule.
models.failure: Treating dashboards as reality instead of instruments.

models.title: A-B-Z Framework
models.summary: Hold a current plan, a near alternative, and a fallback plan at the same time.
models.use_when: Planning a career move, project bet, business idea, or migration path.
questions: What is Plan A?
What evidence would move me to Plan B?
What is the survival fallback?
What trigger forces a switch?
models.action: Define Plan A, Plan B, Plan Z, and the measurable trigger between them.
models.failure: Using Plan Z as an excuse to avoid committing to Plan A.

models.title: Personal SWOT
models.summary: Map strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats before choosing a path.
models.use_when: You need a grounded view of fit, positioning, or personal strategy.
questions: What advantage do I repeatedly underuse?
What weakness keeps recurring?
What opportunity is visible now?
What external threat can I prepare for?
models.action: Create a four-quadrant note and turn one item from each quadrant into an action.
models.failure: Writing flattering traits instead of evidence-backed patterns.

models.title: Input Goals
models.summary: Set goals around actions you control instead of outcomes you only influence.
models.use_when: Outcome goals create anxiety, procrastination, or false failure.
questions: What input can I do daily?
What output should this input influence?
How will I log completion?
What is the minimum viable repetition?
models.action: Convert the outcome into a weekly input quota with a tracking note.
models.failure: Choosing inputs that are busywork rather than causal drivers.

models.title: Pareto Principle
models.summary: A small share of causes often produces a large share of results.
models.use_when: You have too many tasks, clients, features, habits, or study topics.
questions: Which 20 percent creates most of the value?
Which tasks create almost no value?
What can be deleted, delegated, or delayed?
Where is the real bottleneck?
models.action: Rank items by impact and protect the top few from low-value work.
models.failure: Using 80/20 as a slogan without measuring actual contribution.

models.title: Parkinsons Law
models.summary: Work expands to fill the time available for its completion.
models.use_when: Tasks sprawl, deadlines are loose, or perfectionism delays shipping.
questions: What is the smallest useful version?
What deadline would force clarity?
What can be cut without breaking the outcome?
Where am I polishing instead of deciding?
models.action: Set a hard timebox and define the deliverable before starting.
models.failure: Creating artificial urgency for work that actually needs deep thinking.

models.title: Minimum Viable Product
models.summary: Build the smallest artifact that can test a real assumption with a real user.
models.use_when: A project is growing before its core assumption has been tested.
questions: What assumption must be true?
What is the smallest test?
Who can give useful feedback?
What result would invalidate this?
models.action: Define one assumption, one artifact, one user, and one success threshold.
models.failure: Calling a low-quality version an MVP when it does not test the core risk.

models.title: 5/25 Rule
models.summary: Identify the top five priorities and avoid the next twenty until the top five move.
models.use_when: You are scattered across too many goals or side projects.
questions: What are my top 25 goals?
Which five matter most now?
Which attractive goals must become avoid-at-all-costs?
What will I say no to this week?
models.action: Write the top five and an avoid list; review both weekly.
models.failure: Treating the avoid list as temporary guilt instead of a real constraint.

models.title: Compartmentalization
models.summary: Separate contexts so one domain does not leak into every other domain.
models.use_when: Work, study, health, relationships, and admin keep interrupting each other.
questions: Which context is leaking?
What boundary is missing?
What belongs in a capture note, not in my head?
When will this context be reviewed?
models.action: Assign each concern to a specific note, folder, time block, or review loop.
models.failure: Suppressing important signals instead of giving them a proper container.

models.title: Resistance
models.summary: The strongest avoidance often appears near work that matters.
models.use_when: You repeatedly delay writing, publishing, studying, building, or asking.
questions: What task am I circling but not doing?
What emotion appears before avoidance?
What is the next physical action?
Can I reduce the start to two minutes?
models.action: Name the avoided action and start a tiny version immediately.
models.failure: Turning resistance into identity instead of treating it as a signal.

models.title: Antifragility
models.summary: Design systems that can improve from stress, volatility, and small shocks.
models.use_when: A workflow, habit, project, or career path is too fragile under uncertainty.
questions: What stress could make this stronger?
Where is downside capped?
Where is upside open-ended?
What small experiment creates learning?
models.action: Add small controlled stressors, feedback loops, and capped downside bets.
models.failure: Confusing antifragility with recklessness or constant chaos.

models.title: Redundancy
models.summary: Keep spare capacity or backup paths where failure would be expensive.
models.use_when: A single point of failure can break a workflow, project, or life system.
questions: What breaks if this one thing fails?
What backup is cheap now and expensive later?
What dependency needs a fallback?
How often should the backup be tested?
models.action: Create one backup route and schedule a test of it.
models.failure: Adding backup everywhere until the system becomes too heavy.

models.title: Via Negativa
models.summary: Improve a system by removing what harms it before adding more complexity.
models.use_when: More tools, habits, supplements, features, or plans are making things worse.
questions: What can I remove?
What is creating drag?
What would stop making the problem worse?
Which addition is compensating for a bad default?
models.action: Delete or pause one harmful element before adding a new one.
models.failure: Using subtraction as avoidance when a positive action is required.

models.title: Lindy Effect
models.summary: For nonperishable ideas and tools, survival over time is evidence of durability.
models.use_when: Choosing books, practices, concepts, protocols, or long-lived tools.
questions: How long has this survived?
Why did it persist?
Is this domain Lindy-relevant?
What recent alternative has unproven durability?
models.action: Prefer durable primitives when the cost of novelty is high.
models.failure: Rejecting new ideas blindly because old things feel safer.

models.title: Sunk Cost / Concorde Fallacy
models.summary: Past investment should not justify future investment if the forward case is weak.
models.use_when: You keep funding, building, studying, or defending something mainly because you already started.
questions: Would I choose this again today?
What future value remains?
What am I afraid to admit?
What would I recover by stopping?
models.action: Ignore past cost, evaluate future expected value, and define a stop rule.
models.failure: Quitting only because the past feels painful rather than because the future case is bad.

models.title: Halo Effect
models.summary: One positive trait can distort judgment of unrelated traits.
models.use_when: Evaluating people, tools, companies, creators, or your own work.
questions: Which trait is dominating my view?
What evidence is independent of the halo?
What would I think if the brand were removed?
Where might I be overgeneralizing?
models.action: Separate the observed trait from the claim being evaluated.
models.failure: Replacing judgment with cynicism toward anything impressive.

models.title: Commitment Bias
models.summary: Prior commitments can pressure you to stay consistent after facts change.
models.use_when: You defend an old decision, public opinion, project, or identity despite weak evidence.
questions: What would I believe if I had not said this publicly?
What new evidence matters?
What identity is attached to this choice?
What update would be honorable?
models.action: State the new evidence and choose whether to recommit, revise, or exit.
models.failure: Changing positions constantly to avoid accountability.

models.title: Hindsight Bias
models.summary: After an outcome, events can look more predictable than they were.
models.use_when: Reviewing a win, failure, market move, relationship outcome, or project result.
questions: What did I actually know then?
What probability did I assign?
Which signals were ambiguous?
What would improve the next forecast?
models.action: Keep decision logs with predictions before outcomes arrive.
models.failure: Using hindsight to punish uncertainty instead of improving judgment.

models.title: Appeal To Popularity
models.summary: Popularity can indicate attention, not truth or usefulness.
models.use_when: A trend, tool, belief, or creator feels credible mainly because many people agree.
questions: What is the underlying evidence?
Who benefits if I follow the crowd?
Is popularity caused by quality or distribution?
What would I think in private?
models.action: Separate social proof from the actual claim and test the claim directly.
models.failure: Ignoring useful crowd signals just to feel independent.

models.title: Paradox Of Choice
models.summary: Too many options can reduce action quality and increase dissatisfaction.
models.use_when: You are stuck comparing tools, careers, courses, prompts, apps, or plans.
questions: What decision criteria matter?
What options can be removed?
What is good enough?
When does more research stop paying?
models.action: Set criteria, cap options, pick, and schedule a review point.
models.failure: Using choice limits to avoid exploring genuinely different options.

models.title: Leverage
models.summary: Use tools, code, media, capital, people, or processes to multiply output per unit of effort.
models.use_when: A valuable action is repeated manually or limited by personal time.
questions: What repeats?
What can be automated, delegated, documented, or productized?
What asset keeps working after I stop?
What leverage has low downside?
models.action: Turn one repeated action into a reusable asset.
models.failure: Chasing leverage before the base action is valuable.

models.title: Compounding / Snowball Effect
models.summary: Small gains can become large when reinvested consistently over time.
models.use_when: Progress feels too slow, or you need a long-term accumulation strategy.
questions: What can compound here?
What is the reinvestment loop?
What breaks the loop?
How will I measure trajectory rather than mood?
models.action: Define a repeatable input and a compounding asset it improves.
models.failure: Expecting compounding before enough repetitions have occurred.

models.title: Exponential Thinking
models.summary: Some systems change by compounding rates, not linear increments.
models.use_when: Growth, learning curves, network effects, automation, or risk accelerates over time.
questions: What grows with each cycle?
What rate matters?
Where does the curve bend?
What looks small now but scales fast?
models.action: Map the growth loop and identify the variable that changes the rate.
models.failure: Applying exponential assumptions to systems without a real feedback loop.

models.title: Information Arbitrage
models.summary: Value appears when you know something useful before, deeper than, or across domains better than others.
models.use_when: Looking for career edge, content ideas, investing insight, or strategic positioning.
questions: What do I know that this audience does not?
What domain can be translated into another?
What signal is underpriced?
How can I validate the edge?
models.action: Create one artifact that transfers useful knowledge across contexts.
models.failure: Mistaking obscure information for valuable information.

models.title: 10/1 Rule
models.summary: Prefer bets where upside can be much larger than downside.
models.use_when: Choosing experiments, outreach, content, product bets, or learning paths.
questions: What is the downside if this fails?
What is the plausible upside?
Can I cap loss and preserve upside?
How many attempts can I afford?
models.action: Run small downside-capped bets with explicit success and stop criteria.
models.failure: Calling a lottery ticket asymmetric when the odds are unknowable or the downside is hidden.

models.title: Fosbury Flop
models.summary: A change in method can outperform more effort inside the old method.
models.use_when: You are competing in a mature workflow where everyone optimizes the same moves.
questions: What rule is assumed but not required?
What constraint can be approached differently?
What would look strange but legal?
What evidence would prove the new method works?
models.action: Identify one convention and design a small test that violates it without violating the goal.
models.failure: Being contrarian for style instead of performance.
